questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression Using the Alternate Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
questions.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1)(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1
$$

Then, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1={tan}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -1)(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +1)={tan}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the following identities: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }
$$

Next, we expand the parentheses and use the above identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ({tan}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot {tan}^{2}⁡\theta -{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }}\cdot \frac{\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }-\frac{1}{\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }}\cdot \cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }-1 \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ({tan}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )={tan}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(2),$ as follows:

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x=\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

Next, we recall the following identity: 

$$
1-{sin}^{2}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x
$$

Using the above identity, we can further simplify our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-(1-{sin}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x-1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡x}}{\cancel{{sec}^{2}⁡x}}-\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡x-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-2{cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{{sec}^{2}⁡x}-1+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1-2{cos}^{2}⁡x.

$$
\frac{{tan}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1}=\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .

$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)}^{2} & ={(1)}^{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{sec}^{4}⁡x-2{sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot {tan}^{2}⁡x+{tan}^{4}⁡x=1.

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{sec}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{tan}^{4}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ({tan}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }({tan}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{\cancel{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }} \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & =({sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1)-1 \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -2\end{aligned}

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{sec}^{4}⁡x-2{sec}^{2}⁡x+1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x{tan}^{2}⁡x.
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{\color{blue}\sec^2 \theta - \tan^2 \theta} =  \dfrac{1}{\color{blue} 1} = 1
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sec^2 \theta - \tan^2 \theta} = 1.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Simplifying an Expression by Factoring Alternative Forms of the Secant-Tangent Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta -1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}1}{\sec{\theta}+\tan{\theta}} = \dfrac{\color{blue}\sec^2{\theta} - \tan^2{\theta}}{\sec{\theta} + \tan{\theta}}
$$

Next, we can further simplify our expression by factoring the numerator as a difference of squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡\theta -{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}}{\cancel{(\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta +\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta -\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sec\theta + \tan\theta} =  \sec{\theta} - \tan{\theta}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Express $\tan^2 x\sec^2 x - \tan^4 x +1$ in terms of $\sec x$ only.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we recall the different forms of the secant-tangent Identity:

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1) & 1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x \\  & (2) & {tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1 \\  & (3) & {sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite our expression using $(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{4}⁡x+1 & ={tan}^{2}⁡x({sec}^{2}⁡x-{tan}^{2}⁡x)+1 \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡x\cdot (1)+1 \\  & ={tan}^{2}⁡x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can use $(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡x+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\tan^2 x\sec^2 x - \tan^4 x +1 = \sec^2 x.
$$
